title: The wonderful effect of love (Imitation 3.5)
hookLine: love makes every heavy thing light
tomorrow: what should the first words of your day be?

cards: A moving box full of somebody's dishes, three flights of stairs, and the elevator's out. The box weighs what it weighs. Carried for someone you love, though, the climb is a different climb than it would be for a stranger.
The Imitation has a chapter on that strange arithmetic, called The wonderful effect of love, and its answer comes in the opening lines: love makes every heavy thing light.

teach.b: Love is a great thing, the chapter says, a great good in every way. It alone makes every heavy thing light, and bears evenly everything uneven. Look closely at the promise.
Not that the weight disappears. Love carries a burden, it says, and doesn't feel it as a burden, and makes the bitter things sweet.
Then the praise runs on like someone who can't stop: nothing is sweeter than love, nothing stronger, nothing higher, nothing wider, nothing fuller or better in heaven or on earth.
And the reason it gives: love is born of God, and can rest only in God. The First Letter of John says it plainly: "love is of God." Then love in motion.
It runs, it flies, it rejoices. When weary, it isn't worn out; when pressed, it isn't crushed.
Like a living flame, the chapter says, it forces its way upward.
Here's the line to tell a friend tonight: the chapter never says the box gets lighter on the scale. It says the one carrying it changes.

how: Some Christians read this chapter of the Imitation slowly, a few lines at a time, often alongside the First Letter of John.

games.q: what does “the wonderful effect of love” mean?
o: a feeling that makes all your problems vanish
a reward God gives for carrying hard things
love that carries the weight without feeling it

games.q: the wonderful effect of love — tap the pairs.
p: from the First Letter of John

s: the chapter says love makes hard things weigh less
the likely reading. the weight stays; love carries it without feeling it as a burden.
the chapter says love is born of God and can rest only in God
that's its reason for all the praise.
love, in this chapter, is a warm feeling that comes and goes
the chapter shows it running and carrying: pressed, but not crushed.

games.q: your cousin is caring for her dad after his surgery, the same chores every night. she says, 'if I loved him more, this wouldn't feel heavy.' what fits the Imitation?
o: she's right: real love makes the work feel easy.
love doesn't remove the weight; it changes the carrying.
she should stop until it stops feeling heavy.
games.why: love carries a burden, the chapter says, and doesn't feel it as a burden. the weight is real; love changes how it's carried.

practice: Pick up something with a little weight: a bag, a stack of books, a full water bottle. Hold it in both hands for a few slow breaths and notice exactly what it weighs.
Then rest it in your lap, keep your hands on it, and bring to mind one person you'd carry it for; stay with their face until the sit ends. If you pray, you can ask for love enough for the carrying.

wordCard.voice: The wonderful effect of love. The Imitation's chapter on a love that carries a burden without feeling it as one.

carryVoice: Here's your line: love makes light, even though the weight stays exactly the same. Rest well.
